title: Data Structures & Algorithms
blurb: The path from Big-O to dynamic programming and interview performance, ordered by how you should learn it. Each pattern node has real problems; do the must-do nodes first, the rest can wait.

nodes.title: Big-O and complexity
nodes.summary: How cost grows with input size, in time and in memory. Every other node is judged by it, and interviewers expect you to state complexity unprompted.
checklist: Define Big-O, Big-Theta and Big-Omega and say which one interviewers usually mean
Rank O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n) and O(n!) and give one algorithm for each
Distinguish best, average and worst case using quicksort as the example
Drop constants and lower-order terms correctly, and explain when constants still matter
State the space complexity of a solution, including the recursion stack
Estimate whether an approach fits the limits: roughly 10^8 simple operations per second

nodes.title: Analysing real code
nodes.summary: Reading complexity off loops, recursion trees and amortised operations. This is how you defend a solution's cost in the interview instead of guessing.
checklist: Derive the cost of nested loops where the inner bound depends on the outer index
Draw a recursion tree for naive Fibonacci and explain why it is O(2^n)
Explain amortised O(1) append for a dynamic array with doubling
Apply the master theorem to merge sort and binary search recurrences
Spot hidden O(n) work inside a loop: slice, indexOf, string concatenation, shift
Explain why a loop that halves n runs O(log n) times

nodes.title: Cost of language built-ins
nodes.summary: The real complexity of the library calls you lean on: array shift, includes, sort, string building, Map and Set. A hidden O(n) call turns an O(n) answer into O(n^2).
checklist: State the cost of push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, slice and includes on a JS array
Explain why repeated string concatenation in a loop can be quadratic in some languages and how to avoid it
Know the sort cost and stability guarantee of your interview language (JS sort is stable since ES2019)
Choose Map over a plain object for frequency counts and explain why
Know the cost of membership checks in a list versus a set
Explain why a queue built on array.shift() is O(n) per dequeue

links.title: Python wiki: time complexity of built-ins

nodes.title: Memory model: stack, heap and references
nodes.summary: How values, references, contiguous arrays and pointer-based structures sit in memory. It explains why arrays are cache-friendly, why linked lists are not, and what 'in place' really means.
checklist: Explain the difference between the call stack and the heap and what lives in each
Explain value versus reference semantics when passing an array to a function
Explain why contiguous arrays beat linked lists in practice (locality of reference)
Define 'in place' and 'O(1) extra space' and say whether the output array counts
Explain how garbage collection reclaims unreachable nodes and what causes a leak
Know the safe integer range in JS and when to reach for BigInt

nodes.title: Recursion
nodes.summary: Base case, recursive case and the call stack that holds them. Trees, backtracking, divide and conquer and DP are all recursion underneath.
checklist: Write the base case first and prove the recursion makes progress towards it
Trace the call stack for a small input by hand
Convert a recursive function into an iterative one with an explicit stack
Explain stack overflow and the practical recursion depth limit in your language
Add memoisation to a recursive function and state the new complexity
Implement fast exponentiation (x^n in O(log n)) recursively

nodes.title: Visualise algorithms
nodes.summary: Watching sorting and data structures run builds intuition faster than reading. Optional, but a good unblocker when a pattern will not click.
checklist: Step through merge sort and quicksort on VisuAlgo and predict each next step
Watch a BST insert and delete, including the two-children delete case
Run BFS and DFS on the same graph and compare the visit order
Trace a small function of your own in Python Tutor to see frames and references

nodes.title: Arrays
nodes.summary: Contiguous memory, index arithmetic and in-place edits. The most common interview input; most patterns later in this roadmap start here.
checklist: Do in-place edits with a write index (move zeroes, remove element)
Rotate an array by k in O(1) extra space with the reversal trick
Build prefix and suffix products to answer product-except-self without division
Use the array itself as a hash map (index marking) for first-missing-positive
Implement Kadane's algorithm for maximum subarray and explain why it works
Handle empty, single-element and all-negative inputs

nodes.title: Strings
nodes.summary: Immutable strings, character counting, parsing and building output efficiently. String questions test edge-case discipline more than cleverness.
checklist: Explain string immutability and build output with an array join or builder
Count characters with a fixed 26-slot array versus a map and say when each fits
Parse a number from a string with sign, whitespace and overflow handling (atoi)
Reverse words in place and handle multiple spaces
Compress a string in place with read and write pointers
Know Unicode pitfalls: code units versus code points in JS strings

links.title: Python wiki: time complexity of built-ins

nodes.title: Matrix traversal
nodes.summary: 2-D arrays: spiral order, rotation, in-place marking and neighbour scans. Shows up on its own and as the input to every grid graph and grid DP problem.
checklist: Walk a matrix in spiral order with four shrinking boundaries
Rotate a square matrix 90 degrees in place (transpose, then reverse rows)
Mark rows and columns to zero using the first row and column as storage
Update a grid in place using encoded states (game of life)
Iterate the 4 or 8 neighbours of a cell with a direction array and bounds check

nodes.title: Hash sets and maps
nodes.summary: Replace an inner scan with an O(1) lookup, and count or group with a map. The single most useful tool for turning O(n^2) into O(n).
checklist: Solve two-sum in one pass with a value-to-index map
Build frequency counts and compare them (anagrams, ransom note)
Group items by a canonical key (sorted string or count signature)
Explain how a hash table works: hashing, buckets, collisions, load factor and resizing
Explain worst-case O(n) lookups and why keys must be immutable or stable
Use a set to find the start of each run in longest-consecutive-sequence in O(n)

nodes.title: Prefix sums
nodes.summary: Precompute running totals so any range sum is one subtraction. Combined with a hash map it counts subarrays with a target sum in O(n).
checklist: Build a prefix-sum array and answer range-sum queries in O(1)
Count subarrays summing to k with a prefix-sum frequency map, seeded with {0: 1}
Handle the modulo variant (subarray sums divisible by k) including negative remainders
Turn 0/1 balance problems into prefix sums by mapping 0 to -1
Build a 2-D prefix sum and query any rectangle with inclusion-exclusion
Explain why sliding window fails with negative numbers but prefix sums still work

nodes.title: Two pointers
nodes.summary: Walk two indexes through the data instead of checking every pair: from both ends on sorted input, or read and write pointers moving the same way.
checklist: Solve pair-sum on a sorted array from both ends and prove no pair is skipped
Extend to 3sum: sort, fix one element, two-pointer the rest, skip duplicates
Explain the greedy argument in container-with-most-water (move the shorter side)
Use read/write pointers to dedupe a sorted array in place
Partition into three groups in one pass (Dutch national flag)
Solve trapping rain water with two pointers and O(1) extra space

nodes.title: Sliding window
nodes.summary: Maintain a moving range and update the answer incrementally instead of recomputing it. Fixed-size and variable-size windows cover most substring and subarray questions.
checklist: Write the fixed-size window template: add the right element, drop the left one
Write the variable-size template: expand right, shrink left while the window is invalid
Track window state with a count map and a 'matched' counter (minimum window substring)
Explain why each index enters and leaves the window at most once, giving O(n)
Recognise when a window does not apply: negative numbers break monotonic shrinking
Solve longest-repeating-character-replacement using window length minus max frequency

nodes.title: Counting windows: at most K and exactly K
nodes.summary: Count subarrays rather than find one: every valid right end contributes (right - left + 1), and 'exactly K' is atMost(K) minus atMost(K - 1).
checklist: Count subarrays with product less than k by adding window length at each step
Derive exactly(K) = atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1) and apply it to binary-subarrays-with-sum
Count substrings containing all required characters by counting valid left starts
Find the minimum-length subarray with sum at least target
Explain why the at-most trick needs a monotonic validity condition

nodes.title: Binary search on sorted data
nodes.summary: Halve the search space each step on any sorted or monotonic structure. Off-by-one bugs here are a classic interview filter, so learn one template and stick to it.
checklist: Write one binary search template with a clear loop invariant and no infinite loops
Find the first and last position of a target (lower bound and upper bound)
Search a rotated sorted array by deciding which half is sorted
Find a peak element using the slope, without a sorted array
Search a 2-D sorted matrix as one flattened array
Avoid overflow with mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 and explain why it matters in Java/C++

links.title: Tech Interview Handbook: sorting and searching

nodes.title: Binary search on the answer
nodes.summary: When checking 'can it be done with X?' is easy and the answer is monotonic in X, binary search X itself. Covers capacity, speed, minimise-the-maximum and split problems.
checklist: Recognise the signal: minimise the maximum or maximise the minimum over a monotonic feasibility check
Pick correct low and high bounds for the answer space
Write the feasibility check in O(n) and state total cost O(n log range)
Solve capacity-to-ship-packages and split-array-largest-sum with the same template
Binary search on a real-valued answer with a fixed iteration count

nodes.title: Stacks: matching, parsing and simulation
nodes.summary: Last-in-first-out for bracket matching, expression evaluation, undo and nested decoding. Any time you need 'the most recent unresolved thing', reach for a stack.
checklist: Match brackets with a stack and a closing-to-opening map
Design a min-stack with O(1) getMin by storing the running minimum
Evaluate reverse Polish notation and explain operand order for - and /
Decode nested strings like 3[a2[c]] with a stack of (count, partial string)
Simulate collisions or path simplification with a stack
Implement a basic calculator with +, -, parentheses and unary minus

links.title: Algorithms, 4th ed.: bags, queues and stacks

nodes.title: Monotonic stack
nodes.summary: A stack kept in increasing or decreasing order answers 'next greater / next smaller element' for every index in O(n). The key to histogram and span problems.
checklist: Find the next greater element for every index in one pass
Handle a circular array by iterating 2n indexes
Choose increasing versus decreasing order from what the question asks
Compute the largest rectangle in a histogram from previous and next smaller bars
Build the smallest number after removing k digits with a greedy monotonic stack
Explain why each element is pushed and popped at most once

nodes.title: Queues, deques and ring buffers
nodes.summary: First-in-first-out for BFS and streaming, and the double-ended queue behind the sliding-window maximum. Know how to build one without O(n) shifts.
checklist: Implement a queue with two stacks and explain the amortised O(1) cost
Implement a queue in JS with a head index or linked list instead of array.shift()
Build a fixed-size circular queue with head, tail and count
Keep a monotonic deque of indexes to get the sliding-window maximum in O(n)
Use a queue to count events in a time window (recent calls)

nodes.title: Linked lists: reversal and fast/slow pointers
nodes.summary: Pointer manipulation without losing nodes: reversal, merging, and fast and slow pointers for middles and cycles. Tests whether you can reason about state carefully.
checklist: Reverse a list iteratively and recursively and state the space cost of each
Use a dummy head to avoid special-casing the first node
Find the middle and detect a cycle with fast and slow pointers
Remove the nth node from the end in one pass with a gap of n
Merge two sorted lists and add two numbers stored as lists
Reverse nodes in groups of k without extra memory

nodes.title: Linked list surgery
nodes.summary: Harder list manipulation: finding the cycle entry, deep-copying with random pointers, sorting a list and splicing sub-lists. Builds the confidence LRU-cache questions need.
checklist: Implement a singly and a doubly linked list class with insert and delete
Find where a cycle starts and explain the maths behind resetting one pointer
Deep-copy a list with random pointers using a map, then with interleaving in O(1) space
Sort a linked list in O(n log n) with merge sort
Check a palindrome list by reversing the second half in place

nodes.title: Sorting algorithms
nodes.summary: Merge sort and quicksort in depth, plus when counting sort or quickselect wins. You rarely hand-write a sort, but interviewers probe stability, worst cases and partitioning.
checklist: Implement merge sort and explain its O(n log n) time and O(n) space
Implement quicksort with Lomuto or Hoare partition and explain the O(n^2) worst case
Explain stability and give a case where it matters
Use counting sort or bucket sort when the key range is small
Use quickselect to find the kth element in average O(n)
Count inversions or reverse pairs by piggybacking on merge sort

nodes.title: Custom comparators and sort-first thinking
nodes.summary: Many problems get easy once the input is sorted the right way. Write correct comparators and know the a - b pitfalls in your language.
checklist: Write a numeric comparator in JS and explain why the default sort is lexicographic
Sort by multiple keys (frequency, then value) with a single comparator
Build the largest number by comparing a+b against b+a as strings
Reconstruct a queue by height by sorting and inserting greedily
Recognise when sorting first turns O(n^2) into O(n log n)

nodes.title: Binary trees: recursive DFS
nodes.summary: Most tree questions are one recursive function returning the right thing from each subtree. Depth, diameter, balance and path sums all use the same shape.
checklist: Write preorder, inorder and postorder traversals recursively
Decide what each recursive call returns versus what it records globally (diameter, max path sum)
Compute height and check balance in one O(n) pass
Compare two trees and check whether one is a subtree of another
Invert a tree and explain the recursion depth on a skewed tree
Solve binary-tree-maximum-path-sum and handle negative values

nodes.title: Level-order traversal (tree BFS)
nodes.summary: Process a tree one level at a time with a queue. The natural fit for right-side view, zigzag order, minimum depth and width questions.
checklist: Write BFS with a queue and process exactly one level per outer loop
Return the right-side view and zigzag order from the same template
Find minimum depth with BFS and explain why it beats DFS there
Compute maximum width using position indexes per level
Group nodes by column for vertical-order traversal

nodes.title: Iterative traversals and tree iterators
nodes.summary: Traverse without recursion using an explicit stack. Interviewers ask for it to check you understand the call stack, and it powers the BST iterator.
checklist: Write iterative inorder traversal with a stack and a current pointer
Write iterative preorder and postorder traversals
Implement a BST iterator with O(h) memory and amortised O(1) next()
Flatten a tree to a linked list in place

nodes.title: Binary search trees
nodes.summary: The ordering invariant gives O(h) search, insert and delete, and an inorder walk returns sorted output. Validation and kth-smallest are interview staples.
checklist: State the BST invariant and validate it with min/max bounds, not just parent comparisons
Search, insert and delete, including deleting a node with two children
Find the kth smallest element with an inorder walk
Build a height-balanced BST from a sorted array
Explain why an unbalanced BST degrades to O(n) and what AVL/red-black trees fix
Recover a BST with two swapped nodes

nodes.title: Lowest common ancestor and path problems
nodes.summary: Find the deepest shared ancestor and reason about root-to-leaf and node-to-node paths. Path sums with a prefix map reuse the subarray-sum idea on trees.
checklist: Find the LCA in a BST using the ordering
Find the LCA in a general binary tree with one postorder pass
Collect all root-to-leaf paths with a target sum using backtracking
Count downward paths with a target sum using a prefix-sum map (path-sum-iii)
Find all nodes at distance k by adding parent pointers and running BFS
Explain binary lifting at a high level for many LCA queries

nodes.title: Build and serialise trees
nodes.summary: Rebuild a tree from traversals and turn a tree into a string and back. Tests whether you understand exactly what each traversal order encodes.
checklist: Build a tree from preorder and inorder using an index map in O(n)
Explain why preorder alone is not enough without null markers
Serialise and deserialise with preorder plus null markers
Build a BST from preorder alone using value bounds
Find duplicate subtrees by serialising each subtree into a map key

nodes.title: Tries
nodes.summary: Prefix trees store strings character by character so prefix lookups cost O(word length). The go-to for autocomplete, word search on a board and XOR maximisation.
checklist: Implement insert, search and startsWith with a map or 26-slot array per node
Support '.' wildcards with DFS over children
Prune a trie while searching a board for many words (word-search-ii)
Return top suggestions per typed prefix (search suggestions system)
Use a binary trie of bits to find the maximum XOR pair
Compare trie memory use against a hash set of all prefixes

nodes.title: Build a binary heap
nodes.summary: A complete binary tree in an array with sift-up and sift-down. JavaScript has no built-in heap, so you may have to write one in the interview.
checklist: Store a heap in an array and compute parent and child indexes
Implement push with sift-up and pop with sift-down, both O(log n)
Explain why heapify of n items is O(n), not O(n log n)
Make a min-heap generic with a comparator so it also serves as a max-heap
Know the heap available in Python (heapq), Java (PriorityQueue) and LeetCode JS

nodes.title: Heaps and top-K
nodes.summary: Priority queues for the k largest or closest items, streaming medians and greedy scheduling. A size-k heap gives O(n log k) where sorting gives O(n log n).
checklist: Keep the k largest with a min-heap of size k and explain the O(n log k) cost
Compare heap, quickselect and bucket sort for top-k-frequent
Maintain a running median with two heaps
Schedule tasks with a max-heap of counts and a cooldown queue
Return k closest points without sorting everything

nodes.title: K-way merge and heap scheduling
nodes.summary: Merge k sorted sources with a heap of their heads, and simulate servers or CPUs ordered by time. Common in senior loops because it mixes heaps with careful bookkeeping.
checklist: Merge k sorted lists in O(N log k) with a heap of list heads
Find the kth smallest in a sorted matrix or among pair sums with a frontier heap
Simulate a single-threaded CPU with a time-ordered and a priority-ordered heap
Use a heap of past choices to undo the worst one (furthest building, refuelling stops)
Find the smallest range covering one element from each of k lists

nodes.title: Graph representations
nodes.summary: Turn edge lists, grids and implicit states into adjacency lists you can traverse. Most graph bugs start with building the graph wrong.
checklist: Build an adjacency list from an edge list with a Map of arrays, directed and undirected
Compare adjacency list, adjacency matrix and edge list on memory and edge lookup
Count in-degrees and out-degrees (town judge)
Model a word or lock state as an implicit graph node with generated neighbours
Represent weighted edges and division ratios as weighted graphs

nodes.title: Graph traversal (BFS and DFS)
nodes.summary: Visit every reachable node exactly once with a visited set. BFS gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS finds components, cycles and paths.
checklist: Write recursive and iterative DFS with a visited set
Write BFS that returns the shortest number of edges from a source
Count connected components in an undirected graph
Detect a cycle in a directed graph with three colours (white, grey, black)
Check bipartiteness with BFS colouring
Clone a graph with a map from old to new nodes

nodes.title: Grid graphs and multi-source BFS
nodes.summary: A grid is a graph whose neighbours are the four adjacent cells. Flood fill, island counting and 'distance to nearest X' via multi-source BFS are interview favourites.
checklist: Flood fill with DFS or BFS and mark visited in place or in a set
Count islands and their areas; explain stack-depth risk on large grids
Run multi-source BFS from every source at once (rotting oranges, 01-matrix)
Solve 'which cells can reach both oceans' by searching backwards from the borders
Find shortest paths in a binary matrix with 8-directional BFS

links.title: Red Blob Games: introduction to A*

nodes.title: Topological sort
nodes.summary: Order the nodes of a DAG so every edge points forward. The answer to any 'prerequisites', 'build order' or 'dependency' question, and it detects cycles for free.
checklist: Implement Kahn's algorithm with in-degrees and a queue
Implement DFS-based topological sort with post-order and reversal
Detect a cycle when Kahn's algorithm processes fewer than n nodes
Find eventually safe nodes by peeling from the sinks
Compute the longest path in a DAG along the topological order (parallel courses)

nodes.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, 0-1 BFS
nodes.summary: Weighted shortest paths. Dijkstra with a heap is the one interviewers expect; know when negative edges or a hop limit push you to Bellman-Ford.
checklist: Implement Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion of stale entries
Explain why Dijkstra fails with negative edge weights
Use Bellman-Ford rounds to respect a limit of k edges (cheapest flights)
Use 0-1 BFS with a deque when weights are only 0 or 1
Adapt Dijkstra to minimise the maximum edge on a path (minimum effort, swim in rising water)
Know Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs on small graphs and its O(V^3) cost

nodes.title: Union-Find
nodes.summary: Disjoint sets with path compression and union by rank answer 'are these connected?' in near-constant time. Ideal for incremental connectivity and redundant edges.
checklist: Implement find with path compression and union by rank or size
Explain the inverse-Ackermann amortised cost in plain words
Detect the redundant edge that creates a cycle in an undirected graph
Merge accounts or equivalent strings by unioning on shared keys
Track component count and component size as unions happen
Choose between union-find and BFS/DFS for a connectivity question

nodes.title: Minimum spanning tree
nodes.summary: Connect every node with the cheapest set of edges. Kruskal (sort edges plus union-find) and Prim (heap) are short to write and come up in network-cost questions.
checklist: Implement Kruskal: sort edges, add each one that joins two components
Implement Prim with a min-heap on a dense point set
Explain the cut property that makes both greedy algorithms correct
Compare Kruskal and Prim on sparse versus dense graphs
Identify critical edges by forcing or excluding each edge and rerunning

nodes.title: Bridges, Euler paths and state-space search
nodes.summary: Tarjan's bridges, Eulerian paths and BFS over (node, visited-mask) states. Rare outside top-tier loops; learn them after everything above feels easy.
checklist: Find bridges with discovery times and low-link values
Construct an Eulerian path with Hierholzer's algorithm (reconstruct itinerary)
Run BFS over (node, bitmask) states to visit all nodes
Model routes as a graph of buses rather than stops (bus routes)

nodes.title: Backtracking
nodes.summary: Choose, explore, un-choose: build candidates one decision at a time and undo each decision on the way back. Subsets, permutations and combinations all share one template.
checklist: Write the choose / explore / un-choose template and say what state is undone
Generate subsets, permutations and combinations and state their output sizes
Skip duplicates by sorting and skipping equal siblings at the same depth
Allow reuse of an element (combination sum) by not advancing the start index
Explain why the complexity is driven by the size of the output
Solve n-queens with column and diagonal sets

nodes.title: Constraint search and pruning
nodes.summary: Backtracking on boards and partitions where pruning decides whether you finish in time. Word search, sudoku and k-equal-partition are the usual suspects.
checklist: Search a board for a word, marking cells visited and restoring them
Generate balanced parentheses by tracking open and close counts
Prune early: sort descending, skip equal failed values, stop when a bucket overflows
Restore IP addresses by bounding segment length and value
Solve sudoku with row, column and box sets

nodes.title: Greedy algorithms
nodes.summary: Make the locally best choice and never look back. Easy to code, hard to justify, so the interview is really about the exchange argument that proves it works.
checklist: Explain the exchange argument for why a greedy choice is safe
Give a counterexample where greedy fails (coin change with odd denominations)
Solve jump game by tracking the furthest reachable index
Solve gas station with a running surplus and a single reset
Partition labels by last occurrence of each character
Use two passes (left-to-right, right-to-left) for candy distribution

nodes.title: Intervals and sweep line
nodes.summary: Sort by start or end, then merge, insert or count overlaps. Calendars, meeting rooms and resource booking all reduce to these few moves.
checklist: Merge overlapping intervals after sorting by start
Insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list in O(n)
Remove the fewest intervals to avoid overlap by sorting on end time
Count the maximum simultaneous overlaps with a sweep over start/end events
Intersect two sorted interval lists with two pointers
Be explicit about whether touching intervals [1,2] and [2,3] overlap

nodes.title: From recursion to tabulation
nodes.summary: The DP recipe: define the state, write the recurrence, memoise it, then flip it into a table and shrink the space. Learn the process once and every DP node gets easier.
checklist: Define a DP state in one sentence ('dp[i] is the answer for the first i items')
Write the recurrence and base cases before any code
Convert top-down memoisation into bottom-up tabulation
Reduce space when each state only depends on the last one or two
Explain overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure with an example
State DP complexity as number of states times work per state

nodes.title: 1-D dynamic programming
nodes.summary: One index of state: stairs, robber, decode ways, word break and coin change. The most frequently asked DP family.
checklist: Solve climbing stairs and house robber with O(1) space
Handle the circular variant (house robber II) by solving two linear cases
Count decodings while handling '0' and two-digit codes correctly
Solve coin change (min coins) and explain why greedy fails
Solve word break with a set of words and dp over prefixes
Track both max and min products for maximum product subarray

nodes.title: Longest increasing subsequence family
nodes.summary: O(n^2) DP over previous elements, then the O(n log n) patience-sorting trick. Unlocks chains, envelopes and divisible subsets.
checklist: Write the O(n^2) LIS DP and explain the state
Write the O(n log n) version with binary search on tails
Count the number of LIS by tracking lengths and counts together
Reduce Russian doll envelopes to LIS with the right sort order
Reconstruct the actual subsequence, not just its length

nodes.title: State-machine DP (stock problems)
nodes.summary: Model each day as a set of states (holding, not holding, cooling down) with transitions. One framework solves the whole buy-and-sell-stock series.
checklist: Draw the state diagram for holding versus not holding
Add a cooldown state and a transaction fee to the same recurrence
Extend to at most k transactions with a dp over (day, k, holding)
Reduce each version to O(1) space per transaction count

nodes.title: 2-D dynamic programming on grids
nodes.summary: Two indexes of state, usually a grid position. Unique paths, minimum path sum and maximal square teach table filling order and rolling rows.
checklist: Count unique paths with and without obstacles
Fill the table in an order where every dependency is already computed
Compress a 2-D table into one rolling row
Solve maximal square with min of three neighbours plus one
Solve dungeon game by filling backwards from the goal

nodes.title: DP on strings
nodes.summary: dp[i][j] over prefixes of one or two strings: LCS, edit distance, palindromes and pattern matching. Edit distance is one of the most asked DP questions.
checklist: Write LCS with dp[i][j] over prefixes and reconstruct the subsequence
Derive edit distance from insert, delete and replace transitions
Find palindromic substrings by expanding around centres and with dp[i][j]
Solve longest palindromic subsequence as LCS of the string and its reverse
Handle '*' and '.' in regular-expression matching
Explain how to reduce O(mn) space to O(min(m, n))

nodes.title: Knapsack patterns
nodes.summary: Pick items under a capacity: 0/1 (each once) or unbounded (reuse). Subset sum, target sum and coin-change-ii are knapsack in disguise.
checklist: Write 0/1 knapsack and explain why the 1-D version iterates capacity backwards
Write unbounded knapsack and explain why it iterates forwards
Count combinations versus permutations by swapping the loop order
Reduce target sum to a subset-sum count
Handle a two-dimensional capacity (ones and zeroes)

nodes.title: Interval DP and tree DP
nodes.summary: dp over ranges [i, j] (burst balloons, cutting sticks) and dp returned up a tree (robber on a tree, cameras). Hard-tier topics that impress when you can name the pattern.
checklist: Define an interval DP state and fill by increasing length
Pick the last action in a range, not the first (burst balloons)
Return a (take, skip) pair from each subtree for house robber III
Assign node states (covered, camera, uncovered) for binary-tree-cameras
Count structurally unique BSTs with a Catalan-style recurrence

nodes.title: Bitmask DP
nodes.summary: Use an integer's bits as the set of items already chosen when n is at most about 20. Rare in product-company interviews.
checklist: Represent a subset as a bitmask and test, set and clear bits
Write dp[mask] transitions and state the O(2^n * n) cost
Recognise the n <= 20 constraint as the signal for bitmask DP
Enumerate all subsets of a mask

nodes.title: Bit manipulation
nodes.summary: XOR tricks, masks and counting set bits. Short questions that test whether you know how integers are stored, including JavaScript's 32-bit quirks.
checklist: Use XOR to find the single non-duplicated number
Count set bits with n & (n - 1) and explain why it clears the lowest set bit
Check a power of two in O(1)
Add two integers without + using XOR and carry
Explain JS bitwise ops as 32-bit signed and use >>> 0 for unsigned results
Build counting-bits in O(n) with dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1)

nodes.title: Math and geometry for interviews
nodes.summary: GCD, primes, modular arithmetic, digit manipulation and a little geometry. Usually a small twist inside a bigger problem rather than the main event.
checklist: Compute GCD with Euclid's algorithm and LCM from it
Generate primes up to n with the sieve of Eratosthenes
Take results modulo 1e9+7 correctly, including subtraction and multiplication
Multiply or add numbers stored as strings digit by digit
Detect overflow when reversing an integer
Compare slopes with a reduced (dy, dx) pair instead of floating point

nodes.title: Segment tree and Fenwick tree
nodes.summary: Range queries with point or range updates in O(log n). Rare in interviews, common in contests; learn it after the core patterns.
checklist: Build a segment tree for range sum and support point updates
Build a Fenwick tree and explain the i & -i trick
Choose between prefix sums (static) and Fenwick/segment trees (with updates)
Count smaller elements after self with a Fenwick tree over compressed values
Explain lazy propagation for range updates at a high level

links.title: USACO Guide: point update range sum

nodes.title: KMP, Rabin-Karp and Z
nodes.summary: Linear-time string matching. Rarely asked; read it if you enjoy it or if a role is search-heavy.
checklist: Build the KMP prefix function and use it to find a pattern in O(n + m)
Implement a rolling hash and explain collision handling in Rabin-Karp
Use a rolling hash to find repeated substrings of fixed length
Compute the Z-array and use it for pattern matching

nodes.title: LRU and LFU caches
nodes.summary: Combine a hash map with a doubly linked list for O(1) get and put. One of the most asked medium questions at product companies, and a real cache policy.
checklist: Implement LRU with a map plus a doubly linked list and sentinel nodes
Explain why a plain map is not enough and what the list adds
Know the shortcut: JS Map preserves insertion order, Java has LinkedHashMap
Implement LFU with frequency buckets and a min-frequency pointer
Explain where LRU is used in real systems (Redis eviction, CDNs, OS page cache)

nodes.title: Design-a-class problems
nodes.summary: Build a small API (browser history, time-based store, Twitter feed) by picking the right structures for each operation. Tests judgement more than tricks.
checklist: List each operation and its target complexity before choosing structures
Combine a map with a sorted list or binary search (time-based key-value store)
Use a heap with lazy deletion when items can change priority
Support snapshots by storing per-key version histories
Write a small set of test calls that exercise each method and edge case

links.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview techniques

nodes.title: A repeatable problem-solving process
nodes.summary: Clarify, work examples, state a brute force, optimise, code, then test. Interviewers grade the process as much as the answer.
checklist: Ask about input size, value ranges, duplicates, empty input and expected output format
Work two small examples by hand, including an edge case, before coding
State a brute force and its complexity before optimising
Name the bottleneck and the data structure that removes it
Dry-run your code on an example line by line before saying you are done
Finish with complexity and one improvement you would make with more time

links.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview techniques
Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview cheatsheet

nodes.title: Pattern recognition
nodes.summary: Map problem signals to patterns: sorted input suggests two pointers or binary search, 'contiguous' suggests a window or prefix sum, 'all combinations' suggests backtracking.
checklist: Name the pattern from the constraints (n <= 20, 10^5, 10^9) before reading the whole prompt
Map keywords to patterns: contiguous, sorted, top-k, dependencies, minimise the maximum
Solve a mixed set of unseen problems and label each with its pattern within five minutes
Keep a mistakes log: the pattern you missed and the signal you should have seen
Re-solve missed problems after 3, 7 and 21 days

links.title: Tech Interview Handbook: algorithms study cheatsheet

nodes.title: Communicating while you code
nodes.summary: Think out loud, narrate trade-offs and take hints well. Silent coding that reaches the right answer still scores poorly at most companies.
checklist: Narrate what you are trying and why, especially when stuck
Confirm the approach with the interviewer before writing code
Use clear names and small helper functions so the code reads aloud
Take a hint by restating it and showing how it changes the plan
Admit a bug calmly, find it with a dry run and fix it

links.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview prep

nodes.title: Testing and edge cases
nodes.summary: Find your own bugs before the interviewer does. A short, deliberate list of edge cases is one of the cheapest ways to raise your score.
checklist: Keep a standard edge-case list: empty, one element, duplicates, negatives, max values
Test off-by-one boundaries in loops and binary searches
Check integer overflow and precision for sums and products
Trace pointer and index updates on a three-element example

links.title: Tech Interview Handbook: coding interview cheatsheet

nodes.title: Mock interviews and a practice plan
nodes.summary: Timed mocks with another person, plus a structured list (Grind 75, NeetCode 150) and spaced review. This is where knowledge becomes performance under pressure.
checklist: Follow a fixed list such as Grind 75 or NeetCode 150 in pattern order
Do at least five timed 45-minute mocks with a person, not just alone
Solve medium problems in under 25 minutes before scheduling onsites
Review every mock: what slowed you down and what you would say differently
Practise in the same language and editor you will use on the day
